title: Randomized Quantum Optimal Control
authors: Leeseok Kim, Francisco Riberi, Kevin Baca, Milad Marvian
abstract: Quantum optimal control (QOC) aims to find control functions that optimally steer a quantum system toward a target operation. We introduce a \emph{randomized} QOC framework where optimization is carried over an ensemble of control functions and their probabilities, instead of a single set of functions. Using this framework, we prove that randomized QOC can reach a target accuracy faster than any deterministic protocol under the same resource constraints. We also develop general symmetry-based constructions that convert a given control into an ensemble of controls that can systematically reduce the error. We benchmark these constructions for CNOT implementation and find that the resulting randomized protocol quadratically suppresses the error of the optimized deterministic solution. In addition, we introduce randomized GRAPE, which generalizes GRAPE to directly optimize control ensembles and their associated probabilities. Finally, as a related application, we discuss randomized boundary-pulse constructions {that enhance} robustness against coherent noise.
summary: This paper introduces Randomized Quantum Optimal Control (QOC), a framework where optimization is performed over an ensemble of controls rather than a single path. It proves that this randomization technique allows protocols to reach target fidelities significantly faster and with lower error than deterministic methods by exploiting coherent error cancellation. The results are highly relevant for designing robust quantum gates in physical systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses how to improve quantum optimal control (QOC) protocols beyond deterministic methods by introducing a randomized framework that optimizes over an ensemble of controls.
main_result: Randomized QOC can achieve significantly faster convergence and suppress systematic errors quadratically compared to the best deterministic protocols, even when considering noise robustness.
method: The authors develop theoretical constructions (like symmetry-based twirls and time-reversal pairings) and numerical algorithms (R-GRAPE) to optimize control ensembles and their associated probabilities.
model_or_system: The work analyzes controlling quantum systems governed by Hamiltonians, focusing on implementing target unitaries like CNOT. Error is quantified using the diamond distance ($\|\cdot\|_{\diamond}$) for process fidelity.
key_observables: Diamond-distance error ($\epsilon_{\diamond}(T)$), observable estimation errors ($\langle O angle - \langle O angle_{	ext{ideal}}$), and the relative error generator ($E_\star$).
important_parameters: Total evolution time $T$, amplitude bound $f_{\max}$, number of ensemble members $M$, and noise strength $\eta$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on specific Hamiltonian models, short-time regimes, and the ability to implement symmetry transformations via admissible controls.
figures_summary: Figures compare deterministic vs. randomized error scaling (showing quadratic suppression) and illustrate noise robustness by comparing $O(\eta)$ versus $O(\eta^2)$ error scaling for CNOT implementation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from introducing the core concept of Randomized QOC, developing symmetry-based constructions to systematically reduce errors, benchmarking these methods on two-qubit gates like CNOT, and finally extending the analysis to achieve noise robustness by averaging over boundary pulses.
why_interesting: For AMO physicists working with open quantum systems or quantum optics, this work provides powerful theoretical tools for designing robust control sequences that actively cancel systematic errors arising from imperfect Hamiltonian knowledge or environmental coupling.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic comparison between deterministic and randomized quantum optimal control. (a) Conventional QOC optimizes a single control waveform to approximate the target unitary Utarg. (b) Randomized QOC optimizes an ensemble of control waveforms, shown here with two branches, together with the associated probability dis- tribution. (c) Averaging over the unitaries generated by different controls can yield a quadratically closer approx- imation to Utarg than the deterministic optimum.

FIG. 2: Optimal control of CNOT implementation in the two-qubit model of (28), with J = 1 and fmax = 10. (a) Deterministic GRAPE solution f. (b) Four symmetry- generated branches of (32), obtained by sign flips and time reversal of f, and applied with equal probabilities of 1/4. (c) Diamond-distance error versus total time T. The symmetry-generated protocol suppresses the de- terministic GRAPE error quadratically, closely following [ϵdet ⋄(T)]2 (faint purple guide), and achieves essentially the same performance as randomized GRAPE.

FIG. 3: Noise robustness of CNOT implementation un- der coherent 1-local noise. The randomized composite boundary twirl suppresses the leading coherent-noise con- tribution and achieves O(η2) diamond-distance scaling, whereas the bare CNOT and naive Pauli boundary-twirl protocols exhibit O(η) scaling.
